E2.question: What evidence is relevant to understanding how Academic impairment (aca_impa) can contribute to an elevated screening-model prediction in college students, without treating it as a causal diagnosis?
E2.answer: Screening teams may utilize poor academic progress as one of several indicators when identifying students who require mental health supports. The literature suggests that mental health problems among college students can negatively impact academic endeavors and overall academic performance. Conversely, research indicates that students who report average to high levels of well-being experience better long-term outcomes, including academic success, regardless of their reported level of psychological distress. Therefore, academic progress can be viewed as a contributing factor or indicator that, alongside other behavioral or emotional difficulties, may prompt a screening model to flag a student as being at elevated risk.

E6.question: What evidence-based guidance exists for communicating non-diagnostic screening results, stating limitations, and suggesting referral/support pathways for college students without providing treatment prescriptions?

Following this evaluation, the recommended pathway is to refer the student to available counseling services. DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. 3 School mental health screening is defined as the use of a systematic tool or process to identify the strengths and needs of students. Screening is conducted for all students, not just students identified as being at risk for or already displaying mental health concerns. This might involve screening an entire population, such as a school’s student body, or a smaller subset of a population, such as a specific grade level. Most commonly, mental health screening is used to identify individual students who are experiencing or are at risk of experiencing social, emotional, and/or behavioral difficulties. The use of screening as an early identification strategy detects the onset of challenges early so that they can be addressed before they escalate. Screening measures can also ask students about: • indicators of well-being and positive mental health • life satisfaction • school belonging • social determinants of mental health • adverse early life experiences What is School Mental Health Screening?
